title: Meeting Rooms II
description: Minimum rooms = max simultaneous meetings. Sort starts and ends separately, then sweep with two pointers — a meeting reuses a room iff its start is at or after the next ending. O(n log n).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: given a list of meeting intervals like `[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]`, return the minimum number of conference rooms needed to host them all. So if two meetings overlap in time they need separate rooms, but if one ends before the next starts they can share."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Is the input sorted in any way? (Almost certainly not — that's the first move.)
• Touching meetings — if one ends at 10 and the next starts at 10, can they share a room? (Convention says yes; that flips strict `<` vs `<=`.)
• Are start and end always integers, with `start < end`? Any zero-length meetings?
• Should the answer be the *peak* concurrency at any moment, or some weekly total? (Peak — that's what 'minimum rooms' means.)
• Can the input be empty? Return 0?
sections.why: The 'touching reuses' clarification is the load-bearing one — it's the difference between a room count of `n` and a much smaller number on stacked schedules. The reframe from 'minimum rooms' to 'peak concurrency' is the key conceptual unlock; getting the interviewer to nod at that reframe means you've already solved the hard part of the problem.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n^2) (or worse) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is to walk every integer time point and count how many intervals contain it, then take the max. That's O(n * range) which is awful if times are large. A tighter brute force: for each interval, count how many others overlap it, but that's still O(n^2). The real reframe is to stop thinking about rooms and start thinking about *events* on a timeline — every start is a +1 to concurrency, every end is a -1. The answer is the peak running sum. Let me see if I can compute that without scanning every time point."
sections.why: Two reasons to narrate this. (1) The event-stream reframe is the entire algorithmic insight — once you see meetings as +1/-1 events sorted in time, the problem becomes 'find the peak prefix-sum of a sequence', which is trivially O(n) after a sort. (2) Talking through the time-point scan first makes it obvious *why* you don't need it: only the moments where the running count changes (the actual start/end times) matter.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why decouple starts and ends, and why does the sweep work?
sections.say:
"Two equivalent solutions both unlocked by sorting.

**Approach A (the one I'll code) — two-pointer sweep on decoupled events.** I split the intervals into two arrays: all starts and all ends. Sort each independently. Then walk the starts with pointer `s` while a second pointer `e` tracks the next end. For each start, if `starts[s] < ends[e]` then a new meeting begins before any current one ends — increment `used`, update `rooms = max(rooms, used)`. Otherwise some prior meeting has ended (or touches), so we can reuse its room — advance `e`. The output `rooms` is the peak `used` ever reached.

The weird part is that I sort starts and ends *independently* — pairing is irrelevant. That works because I don't care *which* meeting freed the room, only that *a* room was freed by *some* prior meeting. The pairing back to specific intervals doesn't affect concurrency.

**Approach B — min-heap of end times.** Sort meetings by start. Walk through them; for each new meeting, peek the heap-top (smallest end). If `meeting.start >= heap.top` the earliest-ending meeting has freed its room, so pop and push the new end (reuse). Otherwise push the new end without popping (new room). Final answer is `heap.size`. Same O(n log n), more intuitive to some interviewers because each room is an explicit heap entry with its current end time.

Both use sort to put events in time order; both maintain a single piece of state (the next ending). The two-pointer version is cleaner code; the heap version generalizes more naturally to variants (e.g., 'which room did each meeting go in?')."
sections.why: Sorting is what reduces this to a one-pass scan — without it you'd be doing all-pairs comparisons forever. The independent-sort insight in approach A is the part most candidates miss; saying 'pairing is irrelevant, only the timeline matters' explicitly is what separates a coached answer from a derived one. Naming both approaches and the tradeoff (cleaner code vs. easier to generalize) shows you've actually thought about the family of solutions, not just memorized one.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a canonical mix where rooms are reused, a touching-endpoints case that exercises the strict `<`, and a fully-concurrent case where no reuse is possible.

examples.note: Canonical case — meeting [5,10] ends before [15,20] starts, so room 2 gets reused.
examples.trace:
starts sorted = [0, 5, 15]
ends   sorted = [10, 20, 30]
init rooms=0, used=0, e=0
s=0: starts[0]=0 < ends[0]=10 → new room. used=1, rooms=max(0,1)=1
s=1: starts[1]=5 < ends[0]=10 → new room. used=2, rooms=max(1,2)=2
s=2: starts[2]=15 >= ends[0]=10 → reuse. e=1 (used stays at 2)
loop ends
return 2

examples.note: Touching case — [2,4] ends at 4, then [7,10] starts at 7. Strict `<` lets the room be reused even though they don't actually touch.
examples.trace:
starts sorted = [2, 7]
ends   sorted = [4, 10]
init rooms=0, used=0, e=0
s=0: starts[0]=2 < ends[0]=4 → new room. used=1, rooms=max(0,1)=1
s=1: starts[1]=7 >= ends[0]=4 → reuse. e=1 (used stays at 1)
loop ends
return 1

examples.note: All concurrent — every meeting starts before any has ended; no reuse possible.
examples.trace:
starts sorted = [1, 2, 3]
ends   sorted = [5, 6, 7]
init rooms=0, used=0, e=0
s=0: starts[0]=1 < ends[0]=5 → new room. used=1, rooms=1
s=1: starts[1]=2 < ends[0]=5 → new room. used=2, rooms=2
s=2: starts[2]=3 < ends[0]=5 → new room. used=3, rooms=3
loop ends
return 3

sections.why: Two specific things the trace exposes. (1) Notice that `used` never decrements — it only grows on a 'new room' path. That's fine because we only care about the *peak*, and decrementing on reuse would just be bookkeeping that doesn't affect the answer. (2) On `[[7,10],[2,4]]`, watch the `>=` save us — if we used `>` instead, two meetings that just touch (one ending exactly when another starts) would falsely be counted as concurrent. The strict-vs-non-strict pick is the single most common bug in this problem.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty input `[]` → guard at the top, return 0. Without the guard, sort and loop still run safely but the up-front check is cleaner.
• Single meeting `[[1,5]]` → starts=[1], ends=[5], loop runs once, used=1, rooms=1. ✓
• All non-overlapping `[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]` → each new start finds the next end already past, so we just advance `e` and used stays at 1. Returns 1.
• All identical `[[5,10],[5,10],[5,10]]` → all starts at 5, all ends at 10. starts[0]=5 < ends[0]=10 → +1. starts[1]=5 < ends[0]=10 → +1. starts[2]=5 < ends[0]=10 → +1. Returns 3.
• Touching back-to-back `[[1,5],[5,10],[10,15]]` → starts=[1,5,10], ends=[5,10,15]. Each subsequent start equals the prior end → reused. Returns 1.
• Zero-length meeting `[[5,5]]` → starts=[5], ends=[5]. starts[0]=5 < ends[0]=5? No → e=1. Loop ends with used=0, rooms=0. Hm — that's probably wrong; a zero-length meeting still arguably needs a room. I'd flag this and ask the interviewer.
• Very large schedules — sort is O(n log n) on whatever n is; nothing pathological."
sections.why: The zero-length edge is the kind of question the interviewer might not have considered themselves — surfacing it shows you're stress-testing your own model, not just running the canonical examples. The touching-back-to-back case is a great sanity check that the strict `<` is doing what we want; a single conference room can host a back-to-back schedule with no overlap, and the algorithm returns 1 to confirm.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n log n), dominated by the two sorts (sorting starts and sorting ends). The sweep itself is O(n) — pointer `s` advances n times in the outer loop, and pointer `e` advances at most n times total across all iterations, so the inner work is O(n) amortized. Space is O(n) for the two extracted arrays.

The min-heap variant is also O(n log n) — n insertions/pop-pushes, each O(log n). Same asymptotic class, different constant factor; the two-pointer version usually wins on practical benchmarks because comparisons on a pre-sorted array beat heap operations.

If you wanted to extend this to 'return the actual assignment of meeting → room', the min-heap version is cleaner: each heap entry can carry a room ID, and when you pop you reassign the room to the new meeting. The two-pointer version loses that info because it decouples starts from ends."
sections.why: Naming the amortization on `e` is the right defense against 'isn't there a hidden inner loop?' — `e` is a single pointer that only advances, so its total work across the whole algorithm is bounded by n. The 'which version to pick' tradeoff at the end is what proves you understand both approaches as members of the same family, not as competing memorized recipes. Calling out the room-ID extension is the bonus that shows you can adapt the choice to downstream requirements.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the two-pointer sweep on a real input. The highlighted line is what just ran; state shows the decoupled starts/ends arrays, both pointers, and current `used` vs peak `rooms`. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.
trace: function* trace(input) {
const intervals = input.intervals.map(iv => iv.slice());
yield { line: 1, label: `enter — intervals=${JSON.stringify(intervals)}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]) } };
const n = intervals.length;
yield { line: 2, label: `n = ${n}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'empty input → return 0', state: { intervals: [], n, returns: 0 } };
return;
const starts = intervals.map(x => x[0]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
yield { line: 5, label: `starts sorted = ${JSON.stringify(starts)}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts] } };
const ends = intervals.map(x => x[1]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
yield { line: 6, label: `ends sorted = ${JSON.stringify(ends)} — decoupled from starts`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends] } };
let rooms = 0, used = 0, e = 0;
yield { line: 7, label: 'init rooms=0, used=0, e=0', state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e } };
for (let s = 0; s < n; s++) {

yield { line: 8, label: `outer step: s=${s}, starts[${s}]=${starts[s]}, ends[${e}]=${ends[e]}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
if (starts[s] < ends[e]) {

yield { line: 10, label: `${starts[s]} < ${ends[e]} → new meeting starts before next ends; need another room`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
used++;
yield { line: 11, label: `used → ${used}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
rooms = Math.max(rooms, used);
yield { line: 12, label: `rooms = max(prev, used) → ${rooms}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
} else {

yield { line: 13, label: `${starts[s]} >= ${ends[e]} → previous meeting ended (or touches) → reuse room`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
yield { line: 14, label: `e → ${e} (consume one freed end)`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, s } };
yield { line: 17, label: `return ${rooms}`, state: { intervals: intervals.map(iv => [...iv]), n, starts: [...starts], ends: [...ends], rooms, used, e, returns: rooms } };

notes: The starts/ends arrays are decoupled — pairing is irrelevant; only the timeline of events matters.
Strict `<`: a meeting starting exactly when another ends can reuse the room.
Equivalent min-heap solution: push end times, pop when the next start is ≥ heap top — same O(n log n).
reference.crux: Min rooms = peak concurrency. Sort starts and ends into SEPARATE arrays, then sweep: a start before the next end needs a room, a start at/after it reuses one. The peak count is the answer.
cruxDistractors: Sort meetings by start, then for each check how many earlier meetings have an end after this start, taking the max — O(n^2).
Sort intervals by start and greedily assign each to the first room whose last meeting has ended, scanning the room list each time.
Sweep every integer time point from min start to max end, counting intervals that contain it, and return the max.

alternates.label: Min-heap of end times
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer asks which room each meeting goes in, or when the greedy decoupled-sort feels unintuitive. Each heap entry represents one occupied room; the heap root is the soonest-to-free room. Generalizes cleanly to 'assign meeting → room ID' variants.
notes: Heap size at any point = rooms currently occupied; final size = peak rooms needed.
Pop before push when reusing: if the new start is >= the earliest end, one room has freed up.
In production JS use a proper MinHeap class — the sorted-array simulation is O(n log n) amortized but with high constants.

questions.q: Why can starts and ends be sorted independently?
options: Sorting each separately is twice as fast as one combined sort by pair (since each sub-array is half the comparison work)
We only need the timeline of events, not which start pairs with which end
Independent sorts allow the two pointers to advance simultaneously instead of sequentially, halving wall-clock time
Because pairing intervals at sort time would require an O(n log n) stable sort, but two unstable sorts suffice
questions.explain: Rooms in use is a property of the event timeline — how many starts precede the next end — so which start belongs to which end never enters the count.

options: A meeting ends and we decrement `used` — a freed room becomes available
A new meeting begins before any current one ends — we need an additional room
We skip the current start because no end has yet been reached on the timeline
We pair `starts[s]` with `ends[e]` and remove both pointers' entries from consideration
questions.explain: `ends[e]` is the earliest end not yet used to free a room, so a start before it means nothing has come free — `used++` and `rooms` takes the new max; a room is freed in the `else` branch, where `e++` consumes an end event.

questions.q: Why is the comparison `<` and not `<=`?
options: `<=` would skip starts that exactly match an end, missing them from the sweep entirely
If a meeting starts exactly when one ends, the room can be reused — no new room needed
`<=` would make `e` advance past `s` and cause `ends[e]` to read out of bounds
Because integer endpoints in floating-point JS Numbers can compare unreliably at `===`, `<` is the safer test
questions.explain: Endpoints are half-open here: a meeting starting exactly when another ends can reuse that room, so that case must fall through to the `else` and advance `e` instead of allocating.

options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n + max-endpoint-value)
questions.explain: Sorting dominates; the sweep is linear.

questions.q: The minimum number of rooms equals:
options: The total number of meetings
The maximum number of meetings overlapping at any single moment (peak concurrency)
The number of distinct start times
The longest meeting's duration
questions.explain: You only need as many rooms as the busiest instant requires; reframing 'min rooms' as 'peak concurrency' is the core unlock.

questions.q: In the min-heap approach, what do you store in the heap and what does its size represent?
options: Start times; size = number of meetings seen
End times of in-progress meetings; the heap size at any point = rooms currently in use
Meeting durations; size = total rooms ever opened
Room IDs; size = number of distinct starts
questions.explain: Each live meeting contributes its end time to the heap; the heap's size is exactly the count of rooms occupied right now, and its peak is the answer.

questions.q: For the min-heap approach, why sort the meetings by start first?
options: To make the heap smaller
So you process meetings in time order — when a new one starts you can compare its start to the earliest end (heap root) to decide reuse vs new room
Sorting by start is optional
To break ties by duration
questions.explain: Processing in start order lets each new meeting check the smallest end time (heap root): if start >= that end, pop and reuse; otherwise push a new room.

questions.q: In the heap approach, when a new meeting's start is >= the smallest end on the heap, you:
options: Push the new end and open another room
Pop the finished meeting's end and push the new one — the room is reused, heap size unchanged
Do nothing
Clear the whole heap
questions.explain: The earliest-ending meeting has freed its room, so you pop it and push the new end — reuse keeps the room count flat instead of growing it.

questions.q: In the two-pointer version, why can starts and ends be sorted as separate arrays (pairing discarded)?
options: It is a coincidence that works only on the examples
Concurrency only depends on how many starts precede the next end on the timeline, not on which start pairs with which end
JavaScript requires decoupled arrays
To save memory
questions.explain: Peak concurrency is a property of the event timeline; we only need to know that *some* meeting ended to free a room, never which specific one — so pairing is irrelevant.

exercises.prompt: Fill in two-pointer min meeting rooms.

blanks.hint: advance the ends pointer to free a room

L3.prompt: Implement `minMeetingRooms(intervals)` returning the minimum number of rooms. Log it for `[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]` then `[[7,10],[2,4]]`.
hints: Decouple starts and ends, sort both ascending.
Walk starts with pointer s; for each, advance the ends pointer e when the next end ≤ current start.
